analysis.one_liner: Puts expiration dates on federal energy rules so they die unless agencies re-approve them.
analysis.headline: S. 2427 was introduced in the Senate in July 2025 with no cosponsors and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force the Department of Energy, the federal land and offshore drilling agencies, the surface mining reclamation office, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to put expiration dates on their rules. Every existing covered rule would expire within one year unless the agency head formally extends it after taking public comment; new rules would expire after five years unless the agency head declares them 'net deregulatory.' Any rule that is not extended would simply stop having any effect and be removed from the federal rulebook.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy companies that are regulated by these agencies. Oil and gas producers would see rules on offshore drilling safety, offshore and onshore leasing, and federal land use expire unless actively re-approved. Coal and hardrock mining companies would see surface mining and federal mining rules expire. Utilities and energy traders would see Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rules on electricity and gas markets expire. Appliance makers would see Department of Energy efficiency standards expire. All of these rules would only survive if an agency head takes the time to re-justify each one, every few years, forever.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and utility companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the heads of covered agencies to amend every covered regulation in effect on the date of enactment so that it expires no later than one year after that amendment, and requires new regulations to expire within five years.

An agency head can only extend a rule's expiration date by up to five years, and only after giving the public a chance to comment on the rule's costs and benefits and determining that an extension is warranted.

A new regulation can be exempted from the five-year expiration if the agency head determines it has a 'net deregulatory effect' and notifies the Office of Management and Budget, and a deregulatory amendment can extend a rule's expiration without any public comment requirement.
If a rule is not extended, it ceases to have any effect, the agency may not enforce it, and it must be removed from the Code of Federal Regulations.

analysis.who_pays: The general public. Rules that would be subject to expiration include offshore drilling safety rules, surface mining and mine reclamation rules, federal land energy leasing rules, electricity and natural gas market rules, and household appliance efficiency standards. If those rules lapse, the costs show up as weaker environmental and safety protections, less oversight of drilling and mining on public land, and potentially higher household energy bills if efficiency standards disappear.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary people near drilling, mining, and energy projects

drawbacks.text: The bill applies its one-year expiration to rules issued under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, the agency created after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill to police offshore drilling safety, so offshore safety rules would expire within a year unless individually re-approved.

It applies to Department of Energy rules under part B of title III of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, which are the nation's appliance and equipment efficiency standards; if those lapse, households could face higher energy bills over time.
It applies to Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act rules, which govern how mining companies must reclaim damaged land, so mining cleanup requirements would need repeated re-approval to survive.

Because every rule in six agencies would need periodic re-approval, agency staff would be diverted into re-justifying the existing rulebook indefinitely, and any rule an agency simply fails to process on time vanishes by default.

The bill's supporters argue the current energy rulebook is outdated and burdensome, slowing energy production and raising costs; this bill would force agencies to actively defend every rule rather than leave it on the books permanently.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — making agencies periodically justify their rules — is a real idea, but it is applied here as a default-to-expiration rule across six energy and land agencies. Every offshore drilling safety rule, mining reclamation rule, federal leasing rule, appliance efficiency standard, and electricity market rule would evaporate unless individually re-approved, and the bill makes it easier to keep rules alive by amending them to be weaker than by defending them as they are. For energy companies, the benefit is a permanently shrinking rulebook; for the public, the cost is losing established protections by administrative default.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. James Risch introduced S. 2427 in the Senate on July 24, 2025.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, and no further action has been taken since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained — the bill has not advanced, and the existing energy regulations it targets remain in effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill is dormant

for.name: Sen. James E. Risch
for.role: U.S. Senator from Idaho and the bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and secured its referral to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors have joined and no committee or floor votes have occurred, so there is no voting record showing how the parties line up; the only action so far is a Republican sponsor's introduction.

industries.note: Rules governing offshore drilling safety, offshore and onshore leasing, and energy development on federal land would expire within a year unless re-approved, and new rules would lapse in five years unless deemed deregulatory. The industry gains flexibility while the public loses safety and environmental oversight of drilling on public waters and land.

Surface mining and reclamation rules and federal mining rules would be subject to expiration, so requirements to reclaim damaged land and limit mining impacts would need repeated re-approval to survive.

Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rules on electricity and natural gas markets would expire by default; some of these rules protect customers and grid reliability, so utilities gain flexibility in some areas but face uncertainty about which market rules survive.
Department of Energy appliance efficiency standards would expire unless re-approved; manufacturers gain freedom from standards but lose the certainty they often prefer when planning products.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee with no cosponsors and no action for months. Bills in this position — single sponsor, no cosponsors, no committee markup scheduled — almost never receive a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ends, so it is likely to die in committee.
